1965 Shelby Cobra Backdraft Replica Packs a Nasty, Built 427ci V8 and a Five-Speed Manual From Tremc
10 photos
Photo: Garage Kept Motors / Instagram
Sitting proudly in the inventory of Grand Rapids, Michigan-based Garage Kept Motors , this 427 Shelby Cobra will give you "the biggest adrenaline rush you can get with a plate." That’s probably not very far from the truth, if you’re into small and nimble two-seat roadsters with big American motors under the hood.
The AC Cobra, mostly known and sold in the United States as the Shelby Cobra, was a sports car produced between 1962 and 1967 by British company AC Cars and featuring a Ford V8 engine under the hood. It quickly gained a cult following, and since the 1980s various replicas have been produced by a huge number of companies, aiming to continue the spirit of the original.
This 1965 Shelby Cobra is a Backdraft Replica that “combines the timeless styling of an iconic American roadster with modern performance and a thoroughly built 427ci V8.” Despite its stated year, it’s quite thoroughly ready for the late 2020s, finished in Sterling Gray with white racing stripes, and featuring the classic proportions of the original along with muscular fender flares, side-exit exhaust pipes, and a stance that easily “captures the spirit of the original Shelby Cobra.”
It has a mere 3,586 miles since it was built, so “this example offers an exciting opportunity to own a high-performance roadster with unmistakable vintage-inspired styling.” Under the hood resides a 427ci V8 featuring Edelbrock aluminum cylinder heads, an Eagle forged crankshaft, and Mahle forged pistons.
The performance components are a strong foundation, but the V8 is also paired with an engaging Tremec five-speed manual transmission, “giving the driver direct control over the power delivery.” The Backdraft Racing platform mixes classic Cobra allure with modern technology, “resulting in a replica that delivers the visual impact of the original while offering a contemporary approach to performance.”
Inside, the black interior emphasizes the roadster's driver-focused ethos, with an open-top configuration mixed with “a straightforward cockpit designed around the essentials of performance driving.” The conclusion is simple: “With its extensively equipped 427ci V8 , Tremec five-speed manual transmission, distinctive Sterling Gray finish, and only 3,586 miles since completion, this 1965 Shelby Cobra Backdraft Replica offers an exciting blend of vintage racing inspiration and modern performance,” according to the dealership.
Of course, this replica isn’t coming to a new garage on the cheap: the company wants no less than $114,900 to part ways with it. But then again, Shelby Cobras have always been an expensive hobby, and no one would expect them to sell on the cheap, instead suspecting foul play rather than an honest surprise. What do you think? Would you make this your latest addition to a growing collection or the start of one?

Heybike Shows Off V1 Pro at EICMA and It's a Promising Entry Level E-Pit Bike for the Market
9 photos
Photo: Heybike
With the appearance of electrification, the world has been flooded with ride after ride powered by nothing but near-silent and clean juice. There’s no branch of mobility or vehicle design that has gotten away either, and one that I’m currently exploring is electric mini dirt bikes or pit bikes.
Considering my re-sparked interest in motorized two-wheelers , I was able to make it out to the 2026 EICMA in Milan, a venue that stands as the largest stage for two-wheeler brands and is home to over 1,000 of them and close to 800,000 visitors over the course of six days. It was here that I witnessed the latest in electric mobility, with one crew in particular surprising me with an electric dirt bike at their stand.
Photo: Heybike Heybike is that team, a brand known for supplying the market with affordable e-bikes that can really go the distance, often seem spotted under delivery fleet service operators. So, walking by their stand at EICMA, I exclaimed when I saw that this brand has an electric pit bike in the lineup.
It’s called the V1 Pro and based on its stats and what it can do for the new rider may just make it all worth while. Then again, once we consider the price tag, it just makes sense to start your electric pit bike journey on a V1 Pro.
At it’s core, the Pro is completed with a mid-mounted motor design, and unlike a whole lot of the other entry level players out there, this motor is built around a 72 V setup, so punchy power is clearly delivered. Couple that with 250 Nm (184 lb-ft) of torque, and you can see why this one may just be worth every penny of its $2,100 price tag.
Photo: Heybike The motor peaks at a whopping 8 kw, or roughly 11 hp, so we clearly have access to ample spunk, more than enough to help us reach a top speed (limited) of 50 mph (80 kph). Ample speed if you ask me, and more than you’l probably need off-road. Currently, off-road is the only place where you can legally ride the V1 Pro.
That’s not a problem, as we can see, as Heybike also mentions that their Pro is capable of tackling hills with as much as 45 degrees inclines.
Yet, none of that means anything if range is utterly dreadful, and for the Pro, Heybike aimed pretty high. According to their website, up to 60 miles (96.5 km) of riding can be achieved with a Pro, and while the real world is sure to yield a different number, even 40-45 miles of riding seems attractive for this price and power point.
Once drained, it can take up to six hours before you’re out riding again, but from what I found out, you can purchase extra packs and double your range and ride time .
Photo: Heybike However, there’s a neat little trick up the V1 Pro’s sleeve that is sure to entice new riders, but also train them. Heybike mentions that there are four power modes in the works of the Pro, and while the first three stand for speeds, the fourth, a sort of overdrive , if you will, is to be called upon for wheelies.
All you have to do is select the fourth speed mode, hit the throttle, and the bike does the rest. There are countless brands out there these days that allow us to attain this trick, but rarely is it packed with a motor that also packs some serious heat.
In the control department, Heybike also ads a couple of extra traits that the average electric pit bike doesn’t include, one of which is the magnetic kill switch mounted to the steering wheel; if you and the bike get separated, it won’t end up in the neighbors yard before smashing into a wall.
Then there are the hydraulic brakes coupled with a hydraulic suspension at the front and rear, both of which play a part in you controlling the bike while riding, but also while catching some light airtime; the setup comes across as being able to do so. At the front, 220 mm rotors are in place, and at the rear, 190 mm.
Photo: Heybike Tires also play a crucial part in control, and on the V1 Pro , Heybike chose to add a tried and tested mullet setup, with a 17-inch wheel at the front, and a 14-inch one at the rear. The front tire rolls in with a 2.8-inch cross section while the rear offers 3.4 inches. Do enjoy the off-road ready knobs on these rubbers.
All that’s really left to do is take one of these puppies out for a spin and go from there. Keep in mind that there have already been some interest in the V1 Pro, and currently, it carries a rating of five stars out of five; there aren’t a whole lot of electric dirt bikes out there that have an unscathed rating.

The Famvan Is a Comfort-Maximizing Camper Van Made for Family Adventures, It's Now for Sale
36 photos
Photo: Beachside Custom Vans
A lot of people who travel by camper van would like to bring their family along on the adventures, but not all have such a comfort-maximizing setup like the one I'd like to share with you today. Meet the Famvan.
The Famvan is a project based on a 2025 AWD Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with a 170" wheelbase. It was created by Beachside Custom Vans, a Jacksonville, Florida-based company specializing in designing and building premium camper vans.
This build was made for a customer with a family of four who didn't end up using it as much as they planned. In fact, it was barely used, and they decided to list it for sale – more info about that at the end of the article.
As always, let's first take a look at the van's exterior. For starters, the van rides on Black Rhino wheels wrapped in BFGoodrich KO3 all-terrain tires.
Beachside Custom Vans went further in upgrading the off-roading capabilities by installing Bilstein struts and an Agile Offroad Premium RIP kit - its key components are front and rear shocks and a custom-rated rear leaf spring pack.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans At the rear, you'll come across an Owl Vans spare tire carrier / ladder combo. Use it to climb on the van, and you'll find an FVC (Flatline Van Co.) Safari rack.
The rack holds five front-facing Baja Designs LP9 Pro light pods (three clear and two amber), a Fiamma F45S awning, and offers a ton of space for attaching gear. You can also use it as a roof deck. What's more, it has two cut-outs for a vent fan and an A/C unit.
Other notable mods are AMP Research powered side steps, AM Auto opening windows with screens, FVC rocker lockers, an ARB air compressor with two connections in the front and back, and power and water hookups. Moreover, Owl Vans hood gas struts make it easier for you to open the hood.
Enter, and a bright, welcoming interior will greet you. The customer opted for an eye-catching design consisting of a mix of white and grain-finished cabinetry, a slatted white oak ceiling with recessed LED light strips, and walls finished with grey woven fabric.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans The look is complemented by white solid surface countertops, some black accents, like the cabinet and drawer handles, and soft blue faux leather couch upholstery.
The interior has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. This setup lets you turn the cabin into a seating area after you've parked the van.
Thanks to their factory swivel bases, the driver and passenger seats can be turned around to face the back of the van. What's more, the builders added a White Top Adventures overhead cab shelf above.
Straight ahead of the entrance, you'll come across a continuation of the front seating area. Beachside Custom Vans fitted two captain's chairs complete with armrests and seatbelts, as well as a Lagun table mount.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans Next, we have the kitchen on the passenger side. It features a deep stainless steel sink with a cover, a portable stove, and a flip-up table for additional counter space.
Two overhead cabinets, four drawers, and a cabinet underneath the sink are available for storage in the kitchen. But you can use even more space in a massive unit on the opposite side.
Besides integrating a Dometic NRX 115 fridge with a tiny freezer compartment, it offers two large closets, two medium-sized drawers, and a large drawer. The latter has heavy-duty slides that hold a Laveo dry-flush toilet.
Finally, most of the time spent in this van (except for when driving) will be spent in the back. Beachside Custom Vans came up with a space-maximizing setup that can be used for both lounging and sleeping.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans During the day, you can spend some time in the lower part of the area, where you'll find two long benches with two large tables in the middle. This is the hang-out spot, perfect for accommodating a large group of people for dinner, playing board games, and more.
You can transform the setup into a sleeping arrangement quite easily and quickly. To do that, you must remove the tabletops, attach them in between the benches to connect them, and rearrange the cushions. The result is a huge bed that can easily accommodate two adults.
However, this isn't the main sleeping arrangement. Above the lounge area, you'll notice what looks like a lower ceiling. It's, in fact, the lower part of an elevator bed that's made to perfectly resemble the ceiling.
At the flip of a switch, you can lower the elevator bed to your preferred height. You can even leave enough space underneath it to create a bunk bed setup to accommodate four people.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Beachside Custom Vans The lounge area sits a bit higher than the rest of the living space. Beachside Custom Vans used the extra height to install a surprisingly long drawer that can be pulled out toward the rear of the van. You'll also notice extra storage space in the form of Van Essential bags attached to the rear doors.
The two benches I mentioned earlier accommodate the utility systems. Power is on the passenger side – the electrical system's highlights are an 800 Ah battery bank paired with a 3,000 W inverter.
You can use three charging sources to keep the batteries topped off: solar power , shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running.
As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a 35-gallon (132-liter) freshwater tank, an 11-gallon (41-liter) greywater tank, a water filtration system, a 4-gallon (15-liter) Bosch water heater, and an outdoor shower with a quick connect fitting.
Photo: Beachside Custom Vans You can rest assured that all-season adventures are possible with this camper van. This is possible thanks to the double 3M Thinsulate insulation and two important systems: a diesel-powered Espar heater that's tapped into the vehicle's fuel tank, and a 12V A/C unit above the kitchen.
The kitchen's backsplash integrates the "command center" for the rig's utilities. It includes three dimmer light switches, a thermostat, charging points, a battery monitor, and switches for the water pump, the electric dump valves for the water tanks, and the elevator bed.
All in all, Beachside Custom Vans took a plain AWD Sprinter van and turned it into a family-friendly home on wheels packed full with luxuries, ready for any adventure you throw at it.
As mentioned initially, the Famvan is looking for a new owner – it's barely used, with its odometer reading just 4,000 miles (6,437 km). According to the company's listing , the asking price is $205,000 (€182,825) – that's about right given the price of an AWD Sprinter platform and all the modifications and additions it has.

Buy This Bentley Continental GT for the Price of a Toyota Camry and People Will Think You're Loaded
14 photos
Photo: Instagram | diamondmotorworks
If you think that life is too short to spend it driving boring cars but don’t necessarily have the funds to buy a brand-new vehicle with an exciting powertrain capable of neck-snapping performance, wrapped in a luxurious package, then we probably have the right car for you.
We are talking about the Bentley Continental GT pictured above, which may still look brand new to the untrained eye, but those who know a thing or two about cars will recognize that it is a first-gen model. This generation came to life between 2003 and 2011, and for what it’s worth, it has aged like fine wine. This applies to both the exterior and the cockpit, as it still exudes quite modern luxury from its pores.
Beneath the skin lies the old Volkswagen Group D1 platform, and while some might argue that it is nothing more than a Passat with a different body, some chassis tweaks, and a punchy engine under the hood, as well as more premium materials, the truth is that it has nothing in common with the mid-size sedan. But it does with another VW: the Phaeton. The luxury sedan from Volkswagen was made from 2001 and 2016, and this iteration also shared its nuts and bolts with the era’s Audi A8.
We cannot mention the latter without reminding you that production recently ended for good. That’s right, after 32 years, the four-ring brand pulled the plug on its flagship sedan. The last copy was made in mid-October, at the Neckarsulm facility in Germany, so the automaker no longer has a rival to the likes of the Mercedes S-Class and BMW 7 Series.
Photo: Instagram | diamondmotorworks So far, Audi has not confirmed a successor, but those who want a large and quite luxurious Audi can get the first-ever Q9. The full-size SUV takes on the Mercedes GLS and BMW X7, and it is offered in multiple configurations. Unofficial intel suggests that a new flagship sedan might be in the making in China, though details about it are are extremely limited.
Now, back to the pictured Bentley Continental GT, which not only shares its underpinnings with the era’s Audi A8 and Volkswagen Phaeton , but also with the Bentley Flying Spur, which was pretty much a four-door sedan version of its luxury grand tourer sibling.
The GT measured 189.3 inches (4,808 mm) in length, 75.5 inches (1,918 mm) in width, and 54.7 inches (1,390 mm) in height. It had a 108.1 inches (2,746 mm) long wheelbase, and weighed almost 5,200 pounds (2,350 kg).
The pictured car is presented in Moonbeam Silver on top of a Saddle Brown leather interior. It features adaptive, load-leveling air suspension, bi-xenon headlights, an automatic-deploying rear spoiler, heated and power-folding side mirrors, parking sensors at both ends, traction control, electronic stability program, and an electronic differential lock.
Photo: Instagram | diamondmotorworks Other features that are being mentioned in the listing include the 14-way power-adjustable seats at the front with heating and memory settings, a leather-wrapped steering wheel, wood trim, a four-zone automatic climate control system, a 6-disc CD changer, satellite navigation, a premium sound system with 12 speakers, Bluetooth connectivity, cruise control, and a Breitling analog clock, among other things.
Every Bentley fan and their pet can tell you that this generation of the Continental GT was offered strictly with the famous W12 engine. The mill has twin turbos and a 6.0-liter displacement, and pumps out 552 hp (560 ps/412 kW) and 479 pound-feet (650 Nm) of torque. The 0-62 mph (0-100 kph) acceleration was dealt with in less than five seconds, and this model could reach over 198 mph (318 kph) flat out.
Now, the 2005 Bentley Continental GT may not break the bank at all when it comes to the buying part compared to the car that it is, because this thing usually fetches from $18,000 to almost $50,000 in today’s used car market in the States. And we are still talking about a luxury-oriented grand tourer with a punchy engine under the hood aimed at daily drives.
However, just because it does not cost a lot of money to buy does not mean that you should if you are on a tight budget. That’s because it has very high maintenance, and to be honest, it is not exactly the most reliable car out there. Not to mention that it is not frugal either, but you already knew that, didn’t you?
Thus, the last things that we will say about the pictured 2005 Bentley Continental GT are that it has only 6,000 miles (~9,700 km) or so under its belt, which means that it is still new, despite being more than two decades old, and that it costs $38,800. And that’s pretty much new range-topping Toyota Camry money.
Is this luxury GT worth the asking price? If you said yes and want to buy it, then you should reach out to the seller, @diamondmotorworks on Instagram. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Diamond Motorworks (@diamondmotorworks)

2 New Hot Wheels Collectibles That Will Make Some of You Happy for Christmas
18 photos
Photo: Mattel Creations
Christmas is just 41 days away! And I don’t want to go anywhere near the mall for a week beforehand. I’d rather enjoy life at a slower pace, at least when I’m not at the racetrack. That’s why I intend to only shop online for all the gifts I need for family, friends and myself.
Starting in November is also a good idea if you want to avoid potential shipping delays or depleting stocks. I always have fun choosing things for my loved ones. It’s just a bit more complicated when I have to find something for myself.
I could go in 100 different directions, but there’s one question that will often stop me in my tracks: “Do I really need this now?” I would love to get a new motorcycle helmet, but I don’t currently have a bike and I can also still use the Ruroc AT4.0 Cobra for next year. Buying a motorcycle doesn’t make sense when it’s snowing outside.
Part of me keeps thinking I should get a cheap turbo replica for the FC RX-7, but I just know getting the right parts will make a world of difference. New speakers will have to wait for a while, too, so I’m back to the simplest of choices: more Hot Wheels for my collection.
Now, the latest item in the Mattel Brick Shop line might not be available in toy stores before Christmas. But you can still pre-order one from your local dealer if you wanted to. The Maserati MC12 will be available as a 1:32nd-scale model, which means you’ll have to go through 259 individual pieces to get the job done.
I’m slightly surprised Mattel didn’t go for the two-tone (white and blue) finish for this first iteration, which isn’t to say the current paint job isn’t instantly recognizable. As always, you get a choice of two different wheel designs plus the 1/64th-scale Hot Wheels replica of the car inside the package.
So far, Ronald Wong’s casting has only had a Premium version, which means this is the first time we’ll be seeing it with a plastic chassis and non-Real Riders wheels. If you don’t want to wait for this Maserati you can always get an older Mattel Brick Shop release or look at what’s coming up on Mattel Creations in a few days!
I’m talking about one “Very Merry VW”: the T1 Rockster ! We have known for some time now that Phil Riehlman’s casting would be this year’s Exclusive Holiday Car. I just didn’t realize it would be available this fast. The diecast manufacturer didn’t use it in 2024 or 2025, and I was slightly worried that it would never return.
I still have the 2023 RLC Exclusive variation tucked away in its blister card. Even though it’s the most common of all the variations on the market (30,000 units ever made), I’m quite tempted to release it from its plastic prison and have it up on my display shelf. The new Holiday variation uses the exact same wheels as all of its predecessors, which I don’t mind given I’m a big fan of this design.
Some of the holiday-specific design elements you’ll notice are the Spectraflame Red paint job, the gift deco, the green suspension setup and the RLC XMS plate on the back. I wonder if “snowy” tires would have made this thing more desirable or if they would have had the complete opposite effect.
I like the Rockster better than some of the special Christmas cars we’ve seen in recent years (like the 1982 Lamborghini Countach LP 500 S or the 1952 Dodge Power Wagon), but doesn’t come close to my all-time favorite. That “award” goes to the 2018 Texas Drive’em , which ditched the two motorcycles in the back in favor of Rudolf the Red-Nosed Reindeer.
Anyway, the “Very Merry VW” goes live on Mattel Creations on November 17, 2026 at 9 AM PT and will cost $28 a pop (with a limit of two units per customer as usual). Something tells me getting one won’t be that difficult, at least if you’re ready for it on the first day.

Hardtail MTBs Are Still In: This Designer Shows Off What His Idea of Cycling Perfection Looks Like
7 photos
Photo: Sergey Fedotov
The decades have been subject to countless designs based around the timeless bicycle. So much so that it can be considered one of the most looked-at of vehicles, next to cars and motorcycles, that is. Well, one thing that all real bicycles have in common is that they started off as a dream or a concept, and today, we dive deeper into one such concept.
Bicycles have been around for over 100 years, and in that time, have been subject to take after take on what it means to be the most efficient and capable machine out there, and it all comes down to the backbone , or frame.
Photo: Sergey Fedotov Frames come in countless shapes, designs, and abilities, not to mention materials or building blocks to give rise to those traits. Some are completed from steel, some from aluminum, and the more exotic ones, from carbon fiber and titanium.
But, most bicycles have always followed the traditional double-diamond frame, with a rhombus shape split into two triangles by a seat post. Road bikes follow this design, and so do gravel bikes and hardtail MTBs. The exception are full-suspension MTBs, which break the rear wheel away from the frame to grant it dampening abilities.
As a result of all these and more, it’s important to note that all bikes are designed for a particular discipline. It’s why you don’t see road bikes flying down mountain sides and grandma cruisers in the same setting. But, it’s also why MTBs don’t excel on roads either.
Photo: Sergey Fedotov Some frames and bicycle designs have sought to bridge the gap between roads and mountainsides, with one of the most recent being the gravel bike. Gravel bikes are somewhere between a hardtail MTB and a road bike, often spotted with drop bars, for an aerodynamic rider position, and a dropped seat stay to soften up the rear.
While the traditional gravel bike doesn’t have a front suspension, these days, some brands have added suspension forks to their gravel bikes. It’s not much – usually about 30 mm or so – but it is enough to help us break away from the tarmac and gravel road and venture a bit deeper into the woods and hit up light trails.
Up until gravel bikes, it was the hardtail that was often the most called-upon of frame styles for the all-around rider, and some brands still use this frame style as the starting point for their very modern bikes. Even Trek, Cannondale, Scott, Giant, and countless others still produce hardtails.
Photo: Sergey Fedotov Often, these bad boys are equipped with a front suspension fork with a minimum of 80 mm and with a lockout function, can be set to transfer all of your pedaling energy into the rear wheel.
That brings us to the concept before us today, one crafted by Sergey Fedotov and built to represent the Stern brand. Stern is a Russian brand that hit the scene back in 2005, so they’ve been around for well over 20 years, and the FVA, as Fedotov calls it, is “ conceived as a special-edition model ,” so we could very well see Stern taking a crack at this one some day.
As we can see, Fedotov called upon the hardtail design to bring the FVA to life, and another trait that I could make out is that it’s built out of nothing but good old carbon fiber. There are no welds anywhere on the bike and long flowing tubes are also a trait of carbon fiber frames. A traditional double-diamond design is present here.
What I can also make out is that Fedotov knows what it takes to craft a solid MTB, integrating a tapered head tube into the mix and designing the frame with a “racing geometry.” It’s also built around 29-inch wheels.
Photo: Sergey Fedotov Fedotov also calls upon some of the industry’s most revered and proven materials . For example, the fork is a RockShox SID SL Ultimate with 100 mm, and the drivetrain is meant to carry the Shimano name. Shimano is also responsible for a pair of hydraulic disc brakes with 180 and 160 mm rotors. Ritchey can also be spotted all over, a name present on the handlebar, stem, and seatpost.
What I found rather interesting is that Fedotov did NOT equip this concept with the most expensive gear out there, leaving some room for growth, which could be a clear indicator that he is designing this one for the masses and not tossing on wallet-wrenching gear. Without the pedals, the entire setup aims for a total weight of 11 kg (24 lbs).
The question is: How much would someone like you and me pay for a concept of this nature? Well, taking into consideration that a carbon fiber frame is called upon, a fork that costs around $1,000, and a drivetrain of around the same price, I’d say that this one would be going for around $5,000, a price that some folks would consider dropping on a carbon fiber hardtail MTB.
How much would you pay for such a ride ?

CaDA Master Audi RS6 Avant Build Review: Performance Wagon Is Even Meaner in 1:8 Scale Brick Form
17 photos
Photo: CaDA
For years, Danish toymaker LEGO has been the undisputed leader of DIY 1:8 scale model cars. Sure, there have been attempts made to upset it by this or that company, but none of them has managed to get on top. But now, a true contender is moving into the spotlight, and things may not be the same for LEGO.
The newcomer's name is CaDA Bricks , and it stems from China. It entered the market about a decade ago, and since that time it has grown to offer people with a passion for assembling toys themselves quite a diverse offering.
CaDA's portfolio includes, at the time of writing, plastic replicas of anything from flowers to buildings, but, as with most other companies of its kind, the backbone of the business seems to be cars. And the most impressive of them all is the Master series.
The equivalent of LEGO's Technic range, the Master series has only a handful of products to offer at the moment. It starts with a rather peculiar set called the Prairie Dogs, based on a kinetic sculpture of a group of prairie dogs by Canadian JK Brickworks, goes through a Goliath bulldozer, a combine harvester, a German Panther tank, and Space Shuttle Discovery, and ends with 1:8 replicas of five cars.
Photo: CaDA That would be an unnamed V12 hypercar, the Mazda RX-7, Mercedes- AMG One, Mercedes-AMG GT3 , and Audi RS6 Avant. I've already had the pleasure of putting together the two Mercedes cars, and I've already had my say on them. This time, however, it's time to have a quick look at the CaDA Audi RS6 Avant, to my knowledge, the only brick replica of the German high-performance wagon available everywhere.
Before I get into it, here's a quick reminder of what the real car is all about. Introduced in its current form some three years ago and recently refreshed for the 2026 model year, the hot wagon is animated by a 4.0-liter V8 engine rocking twin-turbochargers and an eight-speed transmission.
With this setup, it generates 621 horsepower and 627 lb-ft of torque, enough to get it to 62 mph from a standstill in 3.3 seconds. And every single bit of its capabilities is made obvious by the aggressive bodywork that leaves no room for people to wonder if this thing is capable of taking on legacy supercars .
I felt pretty much the same thing once I set my eyes on the completed CaDA scale version, and then some, as the unavoidable lines, cuts, and holes of a brick model kind of make it even meaner than in real life.
Photo: CaDA Before getting to the completed set, though, I had to navigate through the usual complexities of such a set, which conspire to make the assembly process exciting and rewarding, but from time to time difficult and annoying - a strange mix brick builders are extremely familiar with. But let's take things methodically.
The miniature Audi ships in the same kind of spectacular box as the two Mercedes cars that were sent over by CaDA, with the colors, materials, and design working together to give it a premium feel – so much so, in fact, that you could be tempted to keep it after you're done assembling the set.
The big box contains five other, smaller boxes, each containing the numbered bags with parts, and the two books that tell you what plastic piece should go where. These, too, look and feel premium, perhaps much more so compared to the way LEGO does things.
As I set up my working space and begin assembling the Audi, I stumbled upon the same problem I experienced with the two Mercedes cars from CaDA: it's not always crystal-clear which bag is in which box, and at times matching the bags with the individual steps in the instruction books is a bit confusing.
Photo: CaDA Depending on how people like to do such things, this could lead to some of you opening too many bags, needlessly increasing the complexity of the assembly process, as you end up with too many parts that you don't necessarily need at a given time spread all over the workplace.
Just like when it comes to the LEGO Technic, CaDa has this habit of mixing in multiple bags the actual components of the vehicle with the connectors and pins you need at a given time. I have always found this approach, no matter who takes it, a bit confusing, especially for noob builders who venture into the complex world of such sets.
Once one gets the hang of it, though, the assembly process goes as smoothly as you'd expect from a design of this caliber. Generally speaking, the assembly instructions are clear and straightforward, but there may be times when bringing things together may be quite the opposite.
That usually happens towards the end of the build, when various major components of the car, built separately (like the roof, front and rear ends, and doors), need to be placed in the correct position, and the illustrations are not that helpful in revealing what should go where.
Photo: CaDA As with all other CaDA Master builds, the Audi RS6 Avant has some functional elements: the pistons in the faithfully recreated V8 move, the steering works, even if in a peculiar fashion (check the video below this text to see what I mean), the hood and doors open to reveal what hides behind them (including the seats that can be adjusted), and the suspension system moves up and down.
Finished in a dark blue hue with grey plastic strips taking on the role of bright trim, the car is propped on replica wheels with red brake calipers and shod in Continental tires (the most spectacular wheels of the three CaDA sets I've worked on so far). As usual, there are no stickers you need to manually place on some components, only fully printed details, like, say, all the proper badges.
On a technical level, the CaDA Master Audi RS6 Avant comprises 4,663 individual pieces, which, when properly assembled, transform into a performance wagon standing 23.7 inches (60.3 cm) long, 10.2 inches (25.9 cm) wide, and 6.6 inches (16.8 cm) tall.
CaDA launched the set in August of this year, and it's probably something you should consider for your Christmas shopping list , for self or others. If you do, keep in mind that the price for the model has been set at $324.57.

New Rosso Vintage Is Another Stunning Mercedes-AMG G 63 From Carlex Design
16 photos
Photo: Instagram | carlex_vehicles
Just because that we haven’t been extensively covering Carlex Design’s work these past few months does not mean that the tuner has been resting on its laurels. Quite the opposite, in fact, because it has several brand new projects, like the Rosso Vintage pictured below.
Following hot on the heels of Chris Brown’s G-Wagen, which we covered one month ago here , this build is part of the company’s Vintage lineup. And all it takes to see that is a quick look at the exterior design, because it has been altered to somewhat mimic the design of a classic machine. And just so you know, it’s not a pixel rearranging process, because the vehicle you see above is as real as they come.
Unlike other projects from this series, this particular Mercedes-AMG G 63 does not feature numerous chrome accents on the outside. The front bumper, which is new by the way, wears a black look this time around. The same goes for the side steps, the trim on the front fenders, doors, and rear three-quarter panels, and the rear bumper. The same goes for other parts of the exterior. The grille, which is now decorated with the tuner’s logo, has also come from the aftermarket world.
The Carlex Design Rosso Vintage wears red on the lower parts of the body, whereas the upper sections are finished in black. The dual-tone design is joined by a double pinstripe presented in white, and interrupted by a signature on the rear three-quarter panels. By the way, the latter components, as well as the doors, and front fenders, have been extended, and the same goes for the wheel arches, which are now more muscular.
Photo: Instagram | carlex_vehicles For a more serious tone, the tuner has also tinted the front turn signals, and the wheels no longer feature a chrome look, as the outer sections are now finished in black, whereas the central parts have a red look. The tires have partial white walls, and this further contributes to the pictured Mercedes-AMG G 63’s retro look. It’s unknown whether the suspension has been modified, but we can see that the tailpipes are new, and they are now three instead of two on each side.
The full-size spare wheel attached to the rear door, which is on the custom side of things and mirrors the look of the new wheels, must also be mentioned, just like the Carlex emblem on the rear door. These, as well as a few other tweaks, pretty much complete the look on the outside.
Mind you, don’t go anywhere yet, because the cockpit is also fully custom. And it’s not exactly a surprise, is it? After all, Carlex Design is famously know for its fine-crafted interiors, often with exotic hide and other cool and high-end materials, with the quality sometimes exceeding the OEM one.
In this case, the pictured Mercedes-AMG G 63 has tan leather upholstery and some suede inserts on most touchable surfaces. The front seats appear to have been reshaped with extra bolstering, and the headrests are not integrated this time around. But they do feature cushions on them, with the Carlex Design embroidered logo. The tuner’s emblem is also visible on the seatbacks, on the dashboard panel, and probably on other parts of the interior that we cannot see in these pictures.
Photo: Instagram | carlex_vehicles The same tan look has also been applied to the headliner, whereas the grab handles, seatbelts, and a few other things appear to carry over from the stock G-Wagen. There is also plenty of metal trim on deck, as well as some wood-inspired one (or is that real wood?), and for what it’s worth, this build looks absolutely phenomenal both inside and out. This is my opinion, and you can feel free to contradict me in the comments area below.
However, before scrolling down to the comments box, you should keep on reading because we haven’t mentioned the powertrain yet. And to be honest, there is nothing more special here, because Carlex Design is not famously known for boosting the oomph of its projects. But then again, there was a time when they used to leave the exterior of its builds stock, so who knows, maybe they will eventually apply some elbow grease in the future.
As a reminder, the Mercedes-AMG G 63 has a V8 engine with a 4.0-liter displacement and twin turbocharging. The mill produces 577 hp (430 kW/585 ps) with no outside intervention, and is officially rated at 627 lb-ft (850 Nm) of torque. The model needs just 4.3 seconds to hit 62 mph (100 kph) from zero, with no modifications whatsoever, and that’s impressive for a brick-shaped truck with a premium vibe, isn’t it?
It seems that the Carlex Rosso Vintage is looking for a new home, though the Polish tuner hasn’t mentioned any pricing details in the social media posts embedded below. Thus, if you really must have it, then you should reach out to them. Just know that these things usually cost more than the proverbial arm and leg. Simple and Traditional Ford Crown Victoria ST Comes From the Digital Realm, Probably Rocks Turbo V6
11 photos
Photo: jlord8 / Instagram
Currently, the big Detroit Three don’t make nearly as many passenger cars as they used to back in the day. Ford has the Mustang, Chevy has the C8 Corvette, and Dodge has the Charger. Oh, and Cadillac has the CT5 because the smaller CT4 is going bust.
The Ford Motor Company banks on the credibility of the iconic Mustang pony car and sells both coupe and convertible variants with EcoBoost and V8 power under the hood. GM thinks that Chevrolet only needs the high-performance Corvette in its life, with all versions powered by V8s and again with coupe or convertible body styles. There’s also the dying CT4 compact executive sedan and the larger CT5, which is getting a new generation for the Cadillac roster.
As for Stellantis, they sell the traditional Dodge Charger in both sedan and coupe form as the Challenger has been retired, and offer both EV and inline-six turbo Hurricane powertrains. In the near future, GM is moving faster than the others with a reported next-gen Cadillac CT5 sharing its underpinnings with the reborn Chevy Camaro and even a new Buick sedan!
But over at Ford, all is quiet on the passenger car front, except for the occasional hints that the S650 Mustang could get a four-door sedan body style to compete with the larger Dodge Charger more directly. Alas, a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI has other plans.
Jim, a virtual artist known as " jlord8 " on social media, loves messing around with all things CGI from the automotive realm, and he dreams of a Ford car – once again imagining the potential return of the iconic Crown Victoria.
The latter was a nameplate that ran from 1992 through 2012 as a full-size, traditional sedan across two generations. It replaced the Ford LTD Crown Victoria and was positioned above the Ford Taurus as the largest sedan in North America, twinned with the Mercury Grand Marquis. It was especially famous due to the extensive use for law enforcement via the Crown Victoria Police Interceptor version, as well as the long-wheelbase Crown Victoria sedan sold to the taxi cab fleets.
Over the years, this pixel master has attempted on many occasions to bring back the Ford Crown Victoria nameplate, and his latest unofficial, hypothetical design project joins the roster with the looks of a traditional sedan packing Ford’s current ST design language. As such, we feel that it’s only appropriate for a matching powertrain – perhaps the one from the 2027 Ford Explorer ST, a 385-hp and 415 lb-ft of torque 3.0L EcoBoost V6 mill? So, what do you think – yay or nay? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jim (@jlord8)

Custom Ford Raptor R Packs 1,000 Horsepower on Deep Concave Silver Polished 22s and 37-Inch Tires
7 photos
Photo: vossen / Instagram
It's been a rather long minute since we last discussed something shown by custom forged and hybrid forged wheel specialist Vossen , and it's time to make amends to the Miami, Florida-based company. With this 1,000-horsepower Ford F-150 Raptor R, of course.
The Ford F-Series was born as a series of light-duty trucks succeeding the 1941-1948 Ford pickup truck model back in 1948, taking its place between the current mid-size Ford Ranger and the heavy-duty truck series, and including the Super Duty models since 1999. Throughout its history, the most famous monikers have been the F-100 and later the F-150, introduced in 1975.
Widely regarded as one of the best full-size pickup trucks, the F-Series has also brought an important series of records to the Blue Oval – it’s been the top-selling pickup truck line in the United States since 1977 and also the best-selling nameplate, overall, since 1981. That’s almost half a century of continued dominance, which is a massive achievement.
As such, it’s no surprise that the fourteenth generation remains extremely popular, even after setbacks like the failed F-150 Lightning all-electric model. Right now, after the 2024 refresh, the 2027 model year of the Ford F-150 includes the XL model from $38,110, along with the STX, XLT, Lariat, King Ranch, Platinum, Tremor, and Raptor versions, with MSRPs surging to $75,820. Actually, if you want the Ford F-150 Raptor R instead of the regular model with the 450 hp and 510 lb-ft of torque 3.5-liter high-output EcoBoost V6, you will have to pay more.
The 5.2-liter supercharged Predator V8 engine shared with the 2027 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC and the Mustang GT supercar is a package costing another $37,045 on top of the Raptor’s MSRP. Of course, the most powerful engine offered on the F-150 Raptor truck is tuned specifically for this application and develops ‘just’ 720 horsepower instead of 795 or 815 hp like on the Mustangs.
But some folks don’t care that it’s now again below the 2027 Ram 1500 TRX SRT , which has returned with the Hemi V8 under the hood and the 6.2-liter supercharged engine packing 777 horsepower. Instead, all they care about are the looks and capabilities. Most likely that’s the case here, too, as Vossen decided to share the beauty shots of a pristine example dressed in Oxford White and rocking a series of custom enhancements and modifications.
Those include the color-matched front and rear bumpers plus the hood and fender flares, the massive set of LED lights embedded into the front bumper, as well as the matching white Raptor branding. But, of course, the most enticing feature is the wheel and tire package, which consists of 22 by 12-inch Vossen HFX-4 six-lug alloy wheels finished in Silver Polished and shod in massive Toyo Tires 37-inch by 12.5 R22s!
The Vossen HFX-4 hybrid forged alloy wheels have a starting price of $649 each and come with 19 through 24-inch diameters or 9.5 through 13-inch widths, but that’s for the five-lug version. The six-lug variant fitted on the Oxford White Ford F-150 Raptor R are actually cheaper, starting from $525 and are a go for 17-24-inch diameters and 8.5-12-inch widths. This version seen here is also deeply concave, adding to the drama of the build.
Alas, maybe a 1,000-horsepower Ford F-150 Raptor R like this one, as per the description, isn’t your cup of tea, even though now it can make short work of that 777-hp Ram 1500 TRX SRT. No worries, because Vossen also has other stuff to brag about.
If you want a contemporary mid-engine supercar like the 907-hp plug-in hybrid V8-powered Lamborghini Temerario, then you’re in luck because they just showcased the first Viola Parsifae Lambo Temerario featuring the 7Design Aria Carbon kit, and the setup was also tucked on Vossen Forged GEN-22 wheels finished in Dark Smoke.
It was one of the many Vossen-equipped vehicles on the floor at the 2026 SEMA Show in Las Vegas, Nevada, by the way. If you would rather go with a boxy luxury SUV, they also showed us the first Mercedes-AMG G 63 featuring the full Urban Automotive Widetrack kit and tucked on Urban x Vossen UV-9 alloy wheels that pose a shiny contrast against the Inozetek Super Gloss Navy Blue wrap for the body.
Alternatively, we can ogle all day long at an Aston Martin Valhalla on the new Vossen G2-10 wheels featuring the L2 Lip configuration or a Verde British Racing Ferrari Purosangue on Vossen S21-02 three-piece alloy wheels in Polished Gloss Clear and lowered on a set of Novitec suspension components. So, which one is your favorite and why? source_document.body:
I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.
Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.
When it debuted earlier this year , it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.
USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999 , it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.
Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.
And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.
Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.
If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.
Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.
Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.
The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.
I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.
It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.
And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.
Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.
But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.
I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.
But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.
For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.
Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

source_document.body:
Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.
And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.
What Cybercab owners agree to
The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.
The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Here’s what else is in there:
Tesla can change the subscription price with one month’s notice. You pay $29,990 up front, and the car’s usefulness then depends on a monthly fee Tesla sets.
The Cybercab only works inside Tesla-enabled Robotaxi geofences. Driving outside them is prohibited and can be technically blocked, and Tesla “may expand, reduce, relocate, or otherwise modify the operating area at any time.”
Tesla can suspend or cancel the subscription for “unauthorized or inappropriate use.” Three or more “strikeouts” for improper or unsafe use trigger a one-week suspension of autonomous driving, during which the car may not operate. Your payment isn’t prorated.
Tesla can remotely access, locate, restrict, or control the car, place it in a “safe state,” or end your access, and the agreement says those actions don’t give you remedies beyond what’s in the terms.
Tesla collects “Autonomy Data,” including image data from the cabin camera above the rear-view mirror, kept for 30 days by default.
It’s for personal use only. You can’t put your Cybercab on Tesla’s Robotaxi network, Uber, a delivery app, or a rental platform without Tesla’s written authorization.
No wraps, tint, or wheel changes except through Tesla or an authorized provider, or your subscription can be suspended.
That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.
Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps , and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it . Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.
Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X , summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.
Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.
Tesla says the Model Y runs the same thing
This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.
Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027 . The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.
So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.
Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.
Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.
Electrek’s Take
I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.
You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.
A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.
